summary.title: How to Write a Template Engine in Less Than 30 Lines of Code
summary.one_liner: You learn how a minimal Ruby template engine works by translating template lines into a Proc body string and evaluating it, in under 30 lines of code.
takeaways: Templating can be reduced to two rules: lines starting with % are Ruby code, and {{ ... }} interpolates Ruby inside a line.
Start by writing the output as a plain Ruby render method, then generate an equivalent method dynamically from the template.
Build a string of Ruby code line by line: escape double quotes, strip the leading % for code lines, prefix other lines with output <<, and convert {{ }} to #{ }.
Evaluate the generated Proc string, passing variable names in so it can reference data; the mote library is the inspiration and is used in production.
summary.summary: The article explains how templating works by building a small Ruby template engine. It defines two rules (% lines run as Ruby, {{ }} interpolates Ruby), shows a hand-written render method as an intermediate step, then a method generated from the template via a string. The parse function splits the template by line, applies the translation rules, and evals the resulting Proc. It is based on the mote templating library, which the author says is used in production.
